\\dot{q}^i.description: The time rate of change of the generalized position coordinate \( q^i \), representing the generalized velocity along that coordinate.

q^i.name: Generalized Position Coordinate
q^i.unit: m (or equivalent for generalized coordinate, e.g., rad)
q^i.description: A coordinate that describes the configuration of a system. For a system with \( n \) degrees of freedom, there are \( n \) such independent generalized coordinates.

p_i.name: Generalized Momentum
p_i.unit: kg m/s (or equivalent for generalized momentum, e.g., kg m^2/s)
p_i.description: The generalized momentum conjugate to the generalized position coordinate \( q^i \). It is defined via a Legendre transformation of the Lagrangian: \( p_i = \partial L / \partial \dot{q}^i \).

H.name: Hamiltonian
H.description: The Hamiltonian of the system, which for conservative systems is typically the total energy (kinetic energy + potential energy) expressed as a function of generalized coordinates \( q^i \) and generalized momenta \( p_i \), and possibly time \( t \).

\\partial H / \\partial p_i.name: Partial Derivative of Hamiltonian with respect to Momentum
\\partial H / \\partial p_i.description: This term represents how the Hamiltonian (total energy) changes infinitesimally with respect to a change in the generalized momentum \( p_i \). It dictates the corresponding generalized velocity \( \dot{q}^i \).

dual-string-coupling-constant.title: Dual String Coupling Constant
dual-string-coupling-constant.conceptual_definition: The formula \tilde{g}_s = 1/g_s describes the relationship between the 'bare' string coupling constant, \tilde{g}_s, and the physical, observable string coupling constant, g_s. In string theory, the coupling constant determines the strength of interactions between strings. The 'bare' coupling constant is a parameter in the fundamental Lagrangian, while the physical coupling constant is what is measured in experiments and is affected by quantum corrections and the vacuum expectation values of fields, particularly dilaton-like fields. This relation signifies a duality where strong coupling in one description corresponds to weak coupling in the dual description.
dual-string-coupling-constant.intuitive_summary: This formula reveals a duality where a large observable interaction strength (large g_s) implies a weak underlying bare interaction strength (small \tilde{g}_s), and vice versa.
dual-string-coupling-constant.interpretation: The equation \tilde{g}_s = 1/g_s establishes a reciprocal relationship between two measures of the string coupling strength. The variable \tilde{g}_s represents the 'bare' coupling constant, which is an input parameter in the fundamental string theory Lagrangian. The variable g_s, on the other hand, represents the physical or 'effective' coupling constant, which is the quantity that governs the strength of interactions observed in experiments and is subject to renormalization. This inverse relationship is a manifestation of a duality, often referred to as S-duality, where a strongly coupled regime (large g_s) in one formulation of string theory corresponds to a weakly coupled regime (small \tilde{g}_s) in a dual formulation. This duality is particularly important in understanding non-perturbative effects in string theory, where calculations are often intractable in the strongly coupled regime.
dual-string-coupling-constant.symmetry_origin: This relationship is a direct consequence of S-duality (strong-weak coupling duality) in various string theories, including Type IIA and Type IIB string theory. S-duality is a symmetry that exchanges theories with strong coupling to theories with weak coupling, suggesting a deeper, more unified structure of string theory. It arises from the non-trivial vacuum structure and the presence of scalar fields (like the dilaton) whose vacuum expectation values can renormalize the coupling constants.
dual-string-coupling-constant.limits_and_boundary: As the physical coupling constant g_s approaches infinity (strong coupling), the bare coupling constant \tilde{g}_s approaches zero (weak coupling). Conversely, as the physical coupling constant g_s approaches zero (weak coupling), the bare coupling constant \tilde{g}_s approaches infinity (strong coupling). This highlights the predictive power of duality: phenomena that are difficult to study at strong coupling (large g_s) can be understood by transforming to a dual description where the coupling is weak (small \tilde{g}_s).

\\tilde{g}_s.name: Bare String Coupling Constant
\\tilde{g}_s.description: The fundamental parameter appearing in the string theory Lagrangian, representing the intrinsic coupling strength before quantum corrections and vacuum effects are considered. It is typically dimensionless.

g_s.name: Physical String Coupling Constant
g_s.description: The observable coupling constant that determines the strength of interactions between strings in the physical vacuum. It is affected by quantum fluctuations and the vacuum expectation value of scalar fields, such as the dilaton. It is also dimensionless.

position-operator-commutation-different-.title: Commutation relation for position operators in different directions
position-operator-commutation-different-.conceptual_definition: The commutation relation for position operators in different directions, denoted as [ \hat{x}, \hat{y} ] = 0, is a fundamental principle in quantum mechanics. It states that the position operators corresponding to different spatial dimensions, such as the x-axis and the y-axis, commute. This means that the order in which these measurements are performed does not affect the outcome, and consequently, their corresponding physical quantities can be simultaneously known with arbitrary precision.
position-operator-commutation-different-.intuitive_summary: In quantum mechanics, measuring an object's position along the x-axis and then along the y-axis yields the same result as measuring along the y-axis first and then along the x-axis.
position-operator-commutation-different-.interpretation: In the realm of quantum mechanics, physical observables are represented by operators. The position of a particle along a specific axis is denoted by an operator, such as \( \hat{x} \) for the x-direction and \( \hat{y} \) for the y-direction. The commutator of two operators, \( \hat{A} \) and \( \hat{B} \), is defined as \( [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A} \). A commutator equal to zero, as in \( [\hat{x}, \hat{y}] = 0 \), signifies that the operators \( \hat{x} \) and \( \hat{y} \) commute. This mathematical property has profound physical implications: it means that the observable quantities corresponding to these operators, namely the position along the x-axis and the position along the y-axis, can be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy. In other words, the outcome of measuring the x-coordinate of a particle does not influence the outcome of measuring its y-coordinate, and vice-versa. This is in stark contrast to non-commuting operators, such as the position and momentum operators along the same axis, where the Heisenberg uncertainty principle dictates fundamental limits on simultaneous precision.
position-operator-commutation-different-.symmetry_origin: The commutation relation \( [\hat{x}, \hat{y}] = 0 \) arises from the fundamental assumption of the form of the position and momentum operators in a standard Hilbert space representation of quantum mechanics, often derived from the canonical commutation relations. Specifically, in the position representation, the momentum operator \( \hat{p}_x = -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \) and the position operator \( \hat{x} = x \). When constructing these operators for different Cartesian directions, the spatial derivatives and multiplicative operators act on independent spatial coordinates. The differential operator \( \frac{\partial}{\partial x} \) only acts on the x-coordinate, and the multiplicative operator \( x \) only involves the x-coordinate. Similarly, \( \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \) and \( y \) involve only the y-coordinate. Therefore, applying \( \hat{x} \) then \( \hat{y} \) results in \( \hat{x}\hat{y} = x y \), and applying \( \hat{y} \) then \( \hat{x} \) results in \( \hat{y}\hat{x} = y x \). Since multiplication of classical variables is commutative, \( xy = yx \), their commutator is zero. This reflects the underlying Euclidean symmetry of space, where the choice of coordinate axes is arbitrary, and the concept of position along one axis is independent of the concept of position along a perpendicular axis.
position-operator-commutation-different-.limits_and_boundary: The commutation relation \( [\hat{x}, \hat{y}] = 0 \) is universally valid for all possible states of a quantum system within the standard framework of quantum mechanics, regardless of whether the position coordinates \( \hat{x} \) or \( \hat{y} \) approach zero or infinity. This means that the independence of measurements along orthogonal spatial axes holds true at all scales and for any position values. This contrasts with situations where one might consider approximations or modified quantum theories, but within the standard formulation, this relation is exact and unconditional.

\\(\\hat{x}\\\\(.name: Position Operator along x-axis
\\(\\hat{x}\\\\(.description: The quantum mechanical operator that corresponds to the observable quantity of a particle's position along the x-axis. Its eigenvalues represent the possible measured values of the x-position.

\\(\\hat{y}\\\\(.name: Position Operator along y-axis
\\(\\hat{y}\\\\(.description: The quantum mechanical operator that corresponds to the observable quantity of a particle's position along the y-axis. Its eigenvalues represent the possible measured values of the y-position.

[ A, B ].name: Commutator
[ A, B ].description: The commutator of two operators \( \hat{A} \) and \( \hat{B} \), defined as \( [\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = \hat{A}\hat{B} - \hat{B}\hat{A} \). A commutator of zero implies that the operators commute, meaning the corresponding observables can be measured simultaneously with arbitrary precision.

0.name: Zero
0.description: Represents the mathematical value zero. In this context, a commutator of zero signifies that the operators \( \hat{x} \) and \( \hat{y} \) commute.

spatial-velocity-component.title: Spatial velocity component
spatial-velocity-component.conceptual_definition: The formula defines the spatial component of velocity in a coordinate system. It quantifies how the position of an object changes with respect to time along a specific spatial dimension. This is a fundamental concept in kinematics, describing the instantaneous rate of change of position.
spatial-velocity-component.intuitive_summary: Velocity is the rate at which an object's position changes over time along a particular direction.
spatial-velocity-component.interpretation: The equation defines the $i$-th spatial component of the velocity vector, denoted as $v^i$. It is mathematically expressed as the derivative of the $i$-th spatial coordinate, $x^i$, with respect to time, $t$. The term $dx^i$ represents an infinitesimal change in the $i$-th spatial coordinate, and $dt$ represents an infinitesimal change in time.  Therefore, $v^i$ quantifies how much the object's position along the $i$-th axis changes per unit of time. For instance, if we consider a 3D Cartesian coordinate system, $x^1$ could be the x-coordinate, $x^2$ the y-coordinate, and $x^3$ the z-coordinate. Then, $v^1 = dx^1/dt	ext{ (m/s)}	ext{, } v^2 = dx^2/dt	ext{ (m/s)}	ext{, and } v^3 = dx^3/dt	ext{ (m/s)}$ would represent the velocity components along the x, y, and z axes, respectively.
spatial-velocity-component.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the definition of velocity in calculus and classical mechanics. It is a direct consequence of the definition of the derivative, which measures the instantaneous rate of change. The use of superscripts for velocity components often arises in more advanced contexts like differential geometry or general relativity, where it relates to contravariant vectors. In its simplest form, it is invariant under translations and rotations of the coordinate system, reflecting the physical reality that velocity is an objective property of motion.
spatial-velocity-component.limits_and_boundary: As $dt$ approaches zero, the formula provides the instantaneous velocity. If the spatial displacement $dx^i$ is zero for a finite $dt$, the velocity component $v^i$ is zero, indicating no motion along that axis. If $dt$ approaches infinity while $dx^i$ remains finite, the velocity component approaches zero, implying the object has effectively stopped moving relative to that coordinate over a very long time. In the context of relativistic physics, this formula needs modification due to the behavior of time at speeds approaching the speed of light.

v^i.name: Spatial velocity component
v^i.description: The i-th component of the spatial velocity vector, representing the rate of change of position along the i-th spatial dimension.

x^i.name: i-th spatial coordinate
x^i.description: The i-th spatial coordinate of an object's position in a given reference frame.

dx^i.name: Infinitesimal displacement along the i-th spatial coordinate
dx^i.description: An infinitesimally small change in the i-th spatial coordinate.

dt.name: Infinitesimal time interval
dt.description: An infinitesimally small interval of time.

periodic-potential-energy.title: Periodic potential energy
periodic-potential-energy.conceptual_definition: The formula describes a potential energy function, denoted as \(V\), which varies periodically in space. This type of potential is fundamental in solid-state physics, describing the interaction of electrons with the crystal lattice of a material, or in other contexts where a system experiences repeating forces. The potential has a constant baseline value plus a spatially oscillating component whose amplitude is controlled by a parameter.
periodic-potential-energy.intuitive_summary: This equation models a potential energy that smoothly undulates with a specific spatial pattern, like waves on a surface, built upon a constant background energy.
periodic-potential-energy.interpretation: The potential energy is given by \(V(\mathbf{x}, \epsilon)\), where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the position vector in space (typically 3-dimensional, \(\mathbf{x} = (x, y, z)\)). The term \(V_0\) represents a constant baseline potential energy, often associated with the average potential experienced by a particle or system. The second term, \(\epsilon \cos(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x})\), introduces the spatial periodicity. \(\epsilon\) (epsilon) is a parameter that governs the amplitude or strength of the periodic variation. A larger \(\epsilon\) means deeper potential wells and higher potential barriers. The term \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}\) describes the phase of the cosine function, which depends on the position \(\mathbf{x}\) and the wave vector \(\mathbf{k}\). The wave vector \(\mathbf{k}\) dictates the direction and spatial frequency of the periodic potential; its magnitude, \(|\mathbf{k}|\), determines how rapidly the potential oscillates in space. The cosine function ensures that the potential energy repeats itself at regular intervals dictated by \(\mathbf{k}\), creating a landscape of alternating high and low energy regions.
periodic-potential-energy.symmetry_origin: The periodic nature of this potential energy function implies that the physical system described by it possesses translational symmetry in the direction of the wave vector \(\mathbf{k}\). According to Noether's theorem, continuous symmetries are associated with conserved quantities. While the potential itself is not invariant under arbitrary translations (unless \(\epsilon=0\)), the underlying physics of systems in periodic potentials, such as electrons in a crystal lattice, exhibit discrete translational symmetry, leading to the concept of Bloch's theorem and the quantization of energy into bands.
periodic-potential-energy.limits_and_boundary: As \(\epsilon \to 0\), the periodic term vanishes, and the potential energy becomes constant: \(V(\mathbf{x}, 0) = V_0\). This represents a system with no spatial variation in potential. As \(\epsilon \to \infty\), the amplitude of the periodic variation becomes infinitely large, leading to infinitely deep potential wells and infinitely high potential barriers, a scenario usually unphysical but useful for theoretical modeling of extreme conditions. If \(\mathbf{k}\) approaches zero (i.e., \(\mathbf{k} \to \mathbf{0}\)), the phase \(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{x}\) becomes constant for all \(\mathbf{x}\), and the potential again reduces to \(V(\mathbf{x}, \epsilon) \approx V_0 + \epsilon\), which is a constant potential if \(\epsilon\) is finite. If \(\mathbf{k}\) is very large (high spatial frequency), the potential oscillates very rapidly in space, creating many narrow potential wells and barriers.

V(\\mathbf{x}, \\epsilon).name: Potential Energy
V(\\mathbf{x}, \\epsilon).description: The potential energy of a system as a function of position \(\mathbf{x}\) and the amplitude parameter \(\epsilon\).

V_0.name: Constant Potential Energy
V_0.description: The baseline or average potential energy of the system, independent of spatial position and the periodic modulation.

\\epsilon.name: Amplitude Parameter
\\epsilon.description: A parameter that controls the magnitude of the spatial variation in potential energy. It represents the maximum deviation of the potential from its baseline value \(V_0\).

\\mathbf{k}.name: Wave Vector

\\mathbf{x}.description: The spatial coordinate vector, specifying a point in space where the potential energy is evaluated.
